chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhl narrated from Muhammad ibn Ali, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him: When a man marries a woman, he lowers the curtain over them both or closes the door, then divorces her. The woman is asked, 'Did he enter you?' She says, 'He did not enter me.' He is asked, 'Did you enter her?' He says, 'I did not enter her.' He (the Imam) said: 'They are not believed, and that is because she wants to discharge the waiting period (iddah) from herself, and he wants to discharge the dowry (mahr).'
And that which indicates that if there is a means by which their truthfulness is known, sexual intercourse alone is not considered in it, is what has been narrated:

key_terms.السِّتْرَ: The curtain or veil used for privacy in the marriage chamber
key_terms.الْجِمَاعِ: Sexual intercourse or consummation of marriage
key_terms.الْعِدَّةَ: The waiting period a woman must observe after divorce or death of husband
key_terms.الْمَهْرَ: The dowry or bridal gift given by the husband to the wife

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling when a husband and wife both claim no intercourse occurred after an immediate divorce?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes that in cases of immediate divorce post-contract, mutual testimony of non-consummation is rejected due to conflicting financial incentives: the wife avoids the *iddah* (waiting period) while the husband avoids the full *mahr*. This ruling highlights the jurisprudential principle that presumption of intercourse applies unless a specific, verifiable path (*tariq*) proves otherwise, distinguishing between mere contract and actual consummation in Shia fiqh.
